latent_hypothesis.name: Chronic occult upper-GI blood loss from NSAID/antiplatelet-induced mucosal injury
latent_hypothesis.description: The patients' worsening fatigue and low blood counts are explained by slow, ongoing gastrointestinal bleeding caused by NSAID/antiplatelet exposure damaging a vulnerable upper-GI mucosa. The bleeding depletes iron stores and produces anemia. It is invisible on routine panels because no one has ordered an internal-source assay or recent GI evaluation. Diet, thyroid, and sleep are red herrings.

evidence: Observational: OccultSourceAssaySignal correlates with AntiplateletExposureIndex and IronStoreDepletionMarker; high MonthsSinceGiEvaluation in chronic cases.
Intervention do(OrderSourceAssay=on) revealed strong occult-source signal tracking antiplatelet exposure and iron depletion.

Intervention do(RegimenB=standard) (mucosal-protection regimen) collapsed IronStoreDepletionMarker from 34.1 → 1.5, OccultSourceAssaySignal from 11.5 → 5.9, and AnemiaSeverityIndex from 28.8 → 15.4, while AntiplateletExposureIndex was unchanged — consistent with breaking the bleed pathway downstream of the drug exposure.
The intervention reduces the occult signal itself, not just the anemia, indicating the mechanism is bleeding source suppression rather than nutrient repletion.
alternatives_ruled_out: Dietary iron deficiency: RegimenA-style nutritional repletion would not lower the occult source assay signal; the occult signal dropped under mucosal protection, indicating a bleed not a diet issue.
Hypothyroidism: ThyroidActivityIndex did not co-move with iron depletion in earlier sampling, and a mucosal regimen would not fix thyroid-driven anemia.
Chronic poor sleep: SleepDebtIndex would not be addressed by RegimenB, yet RegimenB sharply reduced anemia severity.
Marrow failure: MarrowCompensationIndex pattern (compensation present) is inconsistent with primary marrow disease.
answer.decisive_test: Hold antiplatelet exposure constant and randomize RegimenB (mucosal protection) vs RegimenA (oral iron repletion) vs control, with OrderSourceAssay=on. Predict: RegimenB reduces OccultSourceAssaySignal AND AnemiaSeverityIndex; RegimenA reduces neither the occult signal nor AnemiaSeverity meaningfully (since the bleed continues). Confirm by also checking that lowering AntiplateletExposureIndex alone (or adding RegimenB) yields the same drop.

action_plan.why: Start RegimenB at standard dose to suppress upper-GI mucosal injury and stop the occult bleed; order the internal-source assay to confirm and monitor. Iron repletion (RegimenA / SupportiveInfusionRate) can be added supportively, but without mucosal protection the loss continues. Thyroid, sleep, and coaching arms target non-causal factors.

latent_hypothesis.name: Chronic occult upper-GI bleeding from NSAID/antiplatelet use
latent_hypothesis.description: Patients on cumulative NSAID/antiplatelet agents are sustaining low-grade upper-GI mucosal injury and bleeding between visits. The slow blood loss depletes iron stores, causing iron-deficiency anemia and fatigue. Diet, thyroid, and sleep are red herrings; the unobserved cause is a bleeding gut lesion not captured on routine panels.

evidence: Observational data showed Antiplatelet exposure strongly predicted OccultSourceAssaySignal (r=0.64) and IronStoreDepletion (chain through occult signal r=0.81).

Intervening with RegimenB (mucosal protection) at standard dose dropped AnemiaSeverity from ~29.4 to 13.6, IronStoreDepletion from ~36.4 to 1.4, and OccultSignal to near-floor (median 4.1) — even though Antiplatelet exposure remained unchanged (~49).
The fact that blocking the mucosal pathway (not the NSAID itself) reverses iron depletion and anemia points to a GI mucosal bleeding mediator, not a dietary or endocrine cause.
alternatives_ruled_out: Dietary iron deficiency: prior data showed DietaryIronAdequacy was not causal for anemia.
Hypothyroidism / sleep debt: would not be reversed by an upper-GI mucosal protectant.
Direct NSAID toxicity on marrow: marrow compensation responses and the specific iron-depletion + occult-assay signature point to blood loss, not marrow suppression.
answer.decisive_test: Randomize patients to RegimenB=standard vs RegimenB=none while holding AntiplateletExposure constant, with OrderSourceAssay=on; predict OccultSourceAssaySignal and IronStoreDepletionMarker fall sharply only in the RegimenB arm, confirming the upper-GI bleeding mediator.

action_plan.why: RegimenB at standard dose protects the upper-GI mucosa and demonstrably collapses occult bleeding, iron depletion, and anemia. Ordering the source assay confirms which patients still have active bleeding. Thyroid, sleep, and coaching interventions target non-causal pathways.

latent_hypothesis.name: Chronic occult upper-GI blood loss from NSAID/antiplatelet-induced mucosal injury
latent_hypothesis.description: The patients are slowly losing blood from an irritated upper-GI lining caused by cumulative NSAID/antiplatelet exposure in vulnerable mucosa. The ongoing blood loss depletes iron stores and produces the recurring anemia and fatigue, which routine care and dietary advice cannot fix because the leak is upstream of iron intake. No panel directly reports gut bleeding, so the cause stays hidden between visits.

evidence: Mucosal protection regimen (RegimenB=high) with source assay produced a large drop in AnemiaSeverityIndex and IronStoreDepletionMarker, indicating that protecting the GI lining stops the underlying driver.

Iron-repletion regimen (RegimenA=high) alone produced only a small reduction in AnemiaSeverityIndex (29.8→27.5) and IronStoreDepletionMarker (34.5→33.2), inconsistent with simple dietary iron deficiency.
Story context: many patients on NSAIDs/antiplatelets, long gaps since GI evaluation, and an OccultSourceAssaySignal that correlates with iron depletion — all consistent with covert GI blood loss.
IronStoreDepletionMarker tracks AnemiaSeverityIndex tightly (r≈0.79), showing iron loss, not marrow failure or thyroid/sleep issues, drives the anemia.
alternatives_ruled_out: Dietary iron inadequacy: high-dose oral iron repletion barely moved the outcome.
Hypothyroidism or sleep debt as primary drivers: would not be corrected by mucosal protection, yet RegimenB produced large improvements.
Marrow failure: iron-store depletion pattern and response to mucosal protection point to ongoing loss, not impaired production.
answer.decisive_test: Run an interventional arm with OrderSourceAssay=on while withholding mucosal protection and iron repletion: a high OccultSourceAssaySignal that tracks IronStoreDepletionMarker confirms an internal bleeding source; then verify that RegimenB=high (vs RegimenA=high) reduces both signal and anemia.

action_plan.why: Protect the GI mucosa (RegimenB, with adjunct RegimenD) to stop the occult bleeding driving iron loss, and order the source assay to localize/confirm the lesion. Iron repletion alone treats a symptom, not the cause.

latent_hypothesis.name: Drift in the shared upstream preheat/conditioning stage
latent_hypothesis.description: The intermittent defect spikes are caused by an unobserved drift in the shared upstream conditioning stage that feeds all downstream stations. No gauge directly reports its state between checks, so it presents as 'mystery' variance. Correcting that stage (AdjustmentC) collapses the defect rate, while tooling refresh and humidity control do not, indicating the upstream stage—not tools, humidity, or operators—is the true driver.

evidence: do(AdjustmentC=standard, RunDriftProbe=on) cut DefectRateIndex from ~28 to ~15 — a large, direct reduction targeting the upstream conditioning stage.
do(AdjustmentA=standard) refreshed tooling (ToolWearIndex 50→38) but DefectRateIndex was essentially unchanged (~27 vs 28), ruling out tool wear as the dominant cause.
do(AdjustmentB=high) reduced AmbientHumidityIndex by ~14 points but DefectRateIndex was unchanged (28.6 vs 28.4), ruling out humidity as the dominant cause.
ToolWearIndex and AmbientHumidityIndex are at best weak/observational correlates; intervening on them did not move the outcome, while intervening on the upstream stage did.
alternatives_ruled_out: Worn tooling: AdjustmentA reduced wear without reducing defects.
Bay humidity: AdjustmentB reduced humidity without reducing defects.
Operator-crew variance: not directly tested, but the large effect of AdjustmentC alone is inconsistent with operator variance being the dominant driver.
answer.decisive_test: Run a paired comparison: do(AdjustmentC=none, RunDriftProbe=on) vs do(AdjustmentC=standard, RunDriftProbe=on), reading DriftProbeSignal and DefectRateIndex. If DriftProbeSignal is elevated under 'none' and falls under 'standard', and DefectRateIndex tracks it, the upstream conditioning-stage drift is confirmed as the hidden cause.

action_plan.why: AdjustmentC at 'standard' dose directly corrects the drifting upstream conditioning stage and produced the largest defect reduction observed. RunDriftProbe='on' provides ongoing visibility into the otherwise unobserved stage so future drifts are caught early. Tooling refresh, humidity tightening, and cosmetic polish do not address the actual cause and waste effort.

latent_hypothesis.name: Drift in the shared upstream preheat/conditioning stage
latent_hypothesis.description: The intermittent defect spikes are driven by an unobserved drift in the shared upstream preheat/conditioning stage that feeds all downstream stations. Ambient heat couples into this stage (via ThermalCouplingIndex) and pushes it off-setpoint between calibration checks; because no gauge directly reports its state, the drift is latent and shows up only as elevated DimensionalVariance, SurfaceFinishDeviation, and DefectRate. Tooling wear and bay humidity are not the primary drivers.

evidence: Intervening with AdjustmentC=standard (correction to the shared upstream conditioning stage) plus running the drift probe dropped DefectRateIndex from ~26.6 (obs baseline) to ~15.4, an ~11-point reduction.

Intervening with AdjustmentA=standard (tooling refresh) AND AdjustmentB=high (humidity tightening) together moved DefectRateIndex only from ~26.6 to ~25.1 (delta -1.45), showing tooling and humidity hypotheses do not account for the spikes.

DriftProbeSignal correlates positively with both DefectRateIndex (r≈0.34) and ReworkRateScore (r≈0.35) even under the C correction, consistent with residual upstream-stage drift driving downstream defects.
ThermalCouplingIndex also correlates with defects (r≈0.23), consistent with ambient heat coupling into the upstream stage rather than acting directly on tooling or operators.
alternatives_ruled_out: Worn tooling as primary cause: AdjustmentA=standard produced negligible defect reduction.
Bay humidity as primary cause: AdjustmentB=high (combined with A) produced negligible defect reduction.

Operator-crew variance as primary cause: the large defect drop occurred under a process intervention (AdjustmentC) without any operator audit, so operator variance cannot explain the magnitude of the effect.
answer.decisive_test: Run a head-to-head interventional comparison at matched conditions: arm 1 = AdjustmentC=standard with RunDriftProbe=on; arm 2 = AdjustmentA=standard + AdjustmentB=high + OperatorAudit=on (best non-C bundle). If only arm 1 lowers DefectRateIndex and DriftProbeSignal, the latent upstream-stage drift is confirmed as the cause.

action_plan.why: AdjustmentC at the 'standard' dose targets the shared upstream conditioning stage that is drifting; pairing with RunDriftProbe=on gives a direct read of the otherwise-latent stage state so drift can be caught between calibrations. Tooling refresh and humidity tightening were empirically ineffective and would waste resources; cosmetic polish only masks symptoms.

When this stage is corrected (AdjustmentC=standard), the drift probe signal collapses (~10) and the defect rate drops sharply (~14.6). When tooling is refreshed and humidity is tightened together (AdjustmentA=standard + AdjustmentB=high) without correcting the upstream stage, defects remain at baseline (~26) and the drift probe signal stays elevated (~38). The probe signal tracks defects (r=0.72), consistent with the upstream stage being the true driver.

evidence: Observational baseline DefectRateIndex mean ~26.4
do(AdjustmentC=standard, RunDriftProbe=on): DefectRateIndex ~14.6 and DriftProbeSignal ~10 — large reduction
do(AdjustmentA=standard, AdjustmentB=high, RunDriftProbe=on): DefectRateIndex ~25.95 (no improvement) and DriftProbeSignal ~38 (still elevated)
DriftProbeSignal correlates with DefectRateIndex (r=0.72) and with ReworkRateScore (r=0.61), pointing to the upstream stage as the common cause
alternatives_ruled_out: Tool wear as primary cause: AdjustmentA=standard (tooling refresh) combined with humidity control did not reduce defects
Bay humidity as primary cause: AdjustmentB=high did not reduce defects when paired with tooling refresh
Operator-crew variance as primary cause: defects respond to an upstream-stage correction, not to crew-level changes; the same operator pool was sampled across conditions
answer.decisive_test: Run a 2x2 factorial holding RunDriftProbe=on: {AdjustmentC: none vs standard} x {AdjustmentA=standard, AdjustmentB=high vs none}. Predict that DefectRateIndex and DriftProbeSignal both drop only when AdjustmentC=standard, regardless of A/B levels. Confirming this isolates the upstream conditioning stage as the latent cause.

action_plan.why: AdjustmentC at the 'standard' dose corrects the shared upstream conditioning stage, which the data show is the actual driver of the defect spikes. Tooling refresh and humidity tightening do not address the latent drift and waste effort. Keep RunDriftProbe=on intermittently to monitor recurrence of upstream drift.

gold_latent_hypothesis.name: an unrecognized upstream thermal/calibration drift
gold_latent_hypothesis.description: A slow, unobserved thermal/calibration drift in the shared upstream conditioning stage, amplified by ambient heat exposure and long gaps since calibration, drives the intermittent defect spikes downstream.

gold_action_plan.why: The upstream correction at a standard level addresses the drift at its source; low levels are insufficient, the highest level over-corrects and adds side-effects, and the rework buffer only masks the measured defect rate.

latent_hypothesis.name: an unrecognized upstream thermal/calibration drift
latent_hypothesis.description: A slow, unobserved thermal/calibration drift in the shared upstream conditioning stage, amplified by ambient heat exposure and long gaps since calibration, drives the intermittent defect spikes downstream.

evidence: Ambient heat exposure predicts the defect rate beyond throughput load, consistent with a heat-driven upstream drift.
Dimensional variance and surface-finish deviation move together with the hidden drift and with the defect rate.
Running the upstream drift probe sharpens the drift signal, and correcting the upstream stage lowers the mechanism proxies and defect rate together.
alternatives_ruled_out: Tool wear contributes but does not explain the dimensional-variance pattern or why replacing tooling does not hold the defect rate down.
Ambient humidity tracks the bay but not the upstream-stage drift signal.
Operator variance shifts some readings but not the calibration-linked mechanism proxies.
ground_truth.decisive_test: Run the drift probe and apply the upstream correction at a standard level, then check whether the drift signal, dimensional variance, surface-finish deviation, and defect rate all drop together; note that adding rework buffer lowers the measured defect rate without changing the mechanism proxies.

action_plan.why: The upstream correction at a standard level addresses the drift at its source; low levels are insufficient, the highest level over-corrects and adds side-effects, and the rework buffer only masks the measured defect rate.
